The view-conditioned model outperforms non-view-conditioned models on validation viewpoints, as non-view-conditioned models incorrectly reconstruct extra semi-transparent voxels near the surface to explain view-dependent phenomena [S2].

The claim is fully supported by the text in Source [S2]. Specifically, Section 8.2 states: 'The results show that the view-conditioned model is better able to model the scene from novel viewpoints. This happens not only because the view-conditioned model can represent some of the viewdependent appearance of the scene, but also because the non-viewconditioned model incorrectly reconstructs extra semi-transparent voxels near the surface of the object to explain view-dependent phenomena.' Additionally, Table 1 confirms that the view-conditioned model outperforms the non-view-conditioned model on validation viewpoints (MSE 85.7 vs 117.8).

This method was introduced in the context of iNGP (Instant Neural Graphics Primitives) to address limitations in capturing complex view-dependent effects [S1].

The claim states that the method was introduced in the context of iNGP to address limitations in capturing complex view-dependent effects. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly mentions 'complicated viewdependent effects' as a problem that reduces rendering quality and causes 'floaters'. It then describes the solution: using a 'larger model' with a 'view-dependent bottleneck size of 256' and a specific '3-layer MLP' structure. This directly supports the claim that the method (the specific MLP structure and bottleneck size) was introduced to address these limitations within the iNGP context.

It is part of the broader effort to improve neural radiance field rendering quality and reduce artifacts like floaters [S1].

The claim states that the effort aims to improve neural radiance field rendering quality and reduce artifacts like floaters. Source [S1] explicitly mentions that complicated view-dependent effects cause 'more floaters' and reduce rendering quality, and states 'We therefore use a larger model' (describing the specific MLP structure) to address this. Thus, the evidence supports the claim that this specific architectural change is part of the effort to reduce floaters and improve quality.

On a human face dataset, view conditioning reduces validation MSE from 117.8 to 85.7 [S2].

The evidence explicitly states in the notes and Section 8.2 that 'View conditioning reduces validation MSE from 117.8 to 85.7 on a human face dataset.' Table 1 also confirms these specific MSE values for the 'Face' dataset under 'No view conditioning' (Val: 117.8) and 'View conditioning' (Val: 85.7).

This method replaces the small bottleneck in Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (iNGP) with a larger view-dependent MLP to better express complex view-dependent effects and reduce the formation of "floaters" (spurious geometry) [S1].

The claim states that a larger view-dependent MLP replaces the small bottleneck in iNGP to better express view-dependent effects and reduce floaters. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this by stating that the original approach causes 'floaters' and encourages optimization to explain away view-dependent effects with them, and therefore they 'use a larger model' with a 'view-dependent bottleneck size of 256' processed by a '3-layer MLP'. All specific details in the claim are present in the evidence.
